PAPER: JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Liu et al Original Paper Bayesian-Based Pharmacokinetic Framework Integrated with Therapeutic Drug Monitoring for Assessing Adherence to Antiseizure Medications: A Clinical Trial Simulation Study Xiao-Qin Liu1, PhD; Zi-Ran Li2, PhD; Wei-Wei Lin3, PhD; Juan Wang1, BSc; Fu-Qing Gu1, BSc; Jun-Jie Ding4, PhD; Zheng Jiao1, PhD 1Department of Pharmacy, Shanghai Chest Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China 2Department of Bioengineering & Therapeutic Sciences, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, United States 3Department of Pharmacy, The First Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University, Fuzhou, Fujian, China 4Center for Tropical Disease and Global Health, Nuffield Department of Clinical Medicine, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom Corresponding Author: Zheng Jiao, PhD Department of Pharmacy Shanghai Chest Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine 241 West Huaihai Road Shanghai 200030 China Phone: 86 15502125571 Email: jiaozhen@online.sh.cn Abstract Background: Adherence to antiseizure medications (ASMs) is a cornerstone of effective epilepsy management. However, current consensus guidelines for assessing medication adherence via therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) may neglect individual patient characteristics, thereby compromising the accuracy of adherence assessments. Objective: This study proposed an innovative Bayesian–based pharmacokinetic (PK) framework integrated with TDM data to address the above limitations, with a focus on 14 widely prescribed ASMs, including brivaracetam, carbamazepine, cloba- zam, eslicarbazepine acetate, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, perampanel, phenobarbital, topiramate, valproic acid, vigabatrin, and zonisamide. Methods: Comprehensive clinical trial simulations were conducted to investigate the PK of ASMs in patients with epilepsy under conditions of full adherence and various nonadherent dosing behaviors, including omission of the last dose and consecutive missed doses. Bayesian posterior probabilities of these dosing behaviors were derived by integrating validated population PK models, individual patient demographics (eg, age, weight, creatinine clearance), dosing history, prior adherence probabilities and TDM measurements. Additionally, the influence of covariates on assessment outcomes was systematically evaluated. Results: The Bayesian-based PK approach demonstrated robust discriminative ability. Under idealized simulation conditions with minimized variabilities, the approach achieved accurate retrodiction of the last 1 or 2 doses across all 14 ASMs and partial retrodiction of extended nonadherence trajectories for 6 ASMs. Concentration thresholds for adherence classification varied significantly across drugs and are influenced by patient-specific factors, comedications, formulation, sampling time, and prior probability. To translate these insights into practice, an adaptable web-based dashboard was developed using the shiny package in R software to enable precise and real-time assessments of medication adherence. Conclusions: This study establishes a Bayesian-based PK approach to enhance the assessment of ASMs adherence. This approach facilitates a paradigm shift from population-based management to patient-specific adherence profiling, offering a practical methodology for the precise evaluation of medication-taking behaviors. JSON: Name: bayesian_pk_tdm_adherence Title: A Bayesian pharmacokinetic–therapeutic drug monitoring framework to quantify patient-specific adherence to antiseizure medications Short Hypothesis: Integrating individual therapeutic drug monitoring measurements with Bayesian posterior inference using validated population pharmacokinetic models and patient covariates will detect missed doses in the last 1–3 dosing events for antiseizure medications with greater accuracy than standard population-based trough-concentration threshold methods. Related Work: Existing approaches to assess antiseizure medication (ASM) adherence rely primarily on population-derived therapeutic ranges for steady-state trough concentrations, self-reporting, pharmacy refill data, or simplified concentration cutoffs. Population pharmacokinetic (PK) modeling and Monte Carlo simulation have been applied to study nonadherence and design remedial dosing, and Bayesian methods have been proposed for compliance estimation from single samples. Limitations of prior work include heavy reliance on adult-average PK parameters that omit pediatric, geriatric, and pregnant pharmacokinetic differences; inadequate incorporation of patient covariates and concomitant drug interactions; sparse treatment of extended-release formulations; sensitivity to residual unexplained variability and assay error; and limited systematic evaluation across multiple ASMs and nonadherence patterns. Few prior systems provide an end-to-end, patient-specific Bayesian pipeline linking validated population PK models, individualized covariates, variable priors, and decision thresholds for multi-drug, multi-population clinical use. Abstract: Accurate identification of recent missed doses of antiseizure medications (ASMs) is critical for clinical decision-making but is hampered by population-based therapeutic ranges that ignore individual pharmacokinetic variability. We propose a Bayesian framework that integrates single-sample therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) with validated population pharmacokinetic models and patient-specific covariates to estimate posterior probabilities of specific recent dosing behaviors (last 1–3 doses taken or missed). The pipeline uses Monte Carlo simulation to compute conditional concentration distributions under competing dosing scenarios and produces concentration–posterior probability mappings and actionable probability outputs. Main contributions are (1) a standardized computational pipeline for multi-drug adherence retrodiction across pediatric, adult, elderly, and pregnant phenotypes; (2) systematic quantification of how covariates, concomitant drugs, formulation, sampling time, assay variability, and priors affect discrimination thresholds; and (3) evaluation against conventional trough-range decision rules. Expected outcomes are improved sensitivity, specificity, and calibrated posterior probabilities for recent nonadherence detection, enabling more precise, patient-specific TDM interpretation and clinical decision support. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Literature-derived population PK parameter sets covering 23 models for 14 ASMs (brivaracetam, carbamazepine, clobazam, eslicarbazepine acetate, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, perampanel, phenobarbital, topiramate, valproic acid, vigabatrin, zonisamide). (2) Simulated cohorts: 40,000 virtual patients per drug per scenario generated by Monte Carlo sampling of covariate distributions: adults (age 40, 70 kg), children (age 8, 25 kg), pregnant women (30 wk, 70 kg), renal function strata eGFR={30,60,90} mL/min/1.73m2, concomitant inducer/inhibitor states, formulation states (IR, ER, suspension), and sampling-time offsets ({-2h, 0, +2h}). (3) External validation: anonymized clinical TDM dataset of ASM trough concentrations with documented dosing histories (target n>=500 samples) if available else synthetic external cohort with added realistic assay error and timing noise. Baselines: (A) 2017 guideline trough therapeutic-range classification (in-range vs out-of-range), (B) fixed single-concentration cutoffs derived from population mean predictions, (C) non-Bayesian population prediction residual test, (D) Bayesian model without individual covariates (covariate-omitted). Metrics: primary—accuracy of retrodiction for last 1, 2, and 3 dosing events (proportion correct); secondary—AUC-ROC, sensitivity, specificity for detecting >=1 missed dose; calibration metrics (Brier score, calibration slope/intercept); median posterior probability for true scenario; distribution of concentration thresholds (mg/L) where posterior probabilities of competing scenarios cross. Experimental setup: implement PK simulations in R with rxode2; set residual unexplained variability (RUV) to three regimes: minimal (additive 0.01 mg/L, proportional 0.1%), moderate (literature-reported RUV), and high (up to 30% proportional); run 1,000 simulation replicates per scenario seeded for reproducibility; compare pipelines by computing metrics aggregated across replicates and stratified by age group, eGFR, concomitant medication, formulation, and sampling-time offset. Ablation studies: (1) remove covariates (age/weight/eGFR) from Bayesian model; (2) vary priors (uniform vs population-informed vs patient-history-informed); (3) vary RUV and assay bias; (4) compare IR vs ER formulation models; (5) evaluate impact of sampling-time error by adding random ±0–4 h misreporting. Statistical analysis: report mean and 95% confidence intervals across replicates; test metric differences vs baselines using paired bootstrap (alpha=0.05). Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: misspecified or incomplete population PK models (missing covariate relationships, metabolite pathways) can produce biased posterior probabilities; mis-estimated RUV or unmodeled assay bias will degrade discrimination and calibration. Data limitations: scarce or low-quality PK models for some ASMs, ER formulations, pediatric subgroups, or pregnant women; lack of sufficiently large, annotated real-world TDM datasets for external validation. Model assumptions: single-sample TDM and assumed dosing history windows (last 1–3 doses) do not capture delayed/partial/extra doses or complex nonadherence patterns. Generalization limits: results may not generalize to populations with comorbidities, severe hepatic impairment, or novel drug–drug interactions absent from source models. Scalability and compute: high-fidelity Monte Carlo posterior computations across many drugs and covariate strata require substantial compute resources for real-time clinical deployment. Operational risks: reliance on accurate reported sampling times and dosing history—errors here critically affect posterior estimates. Regulatory and ethical constraints: clinical use for decision-making requires validation, governance, and transparent uncertainty communication to clinicians.
